A Sunday at El Molinón With My New Friend

Paul Gerald · Profile
Published on October 11, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:05
Instaread

The first thing my seat neighbor said to me at Sporting Gijón was “What a beautiful stadium.” I agreed, and I added it was big for the second division. And it was basically full for a game against Burgos! The sun-drenched stands looked pretty full, with red-and-white stripes all around us. I was happy to find out that she wanted to chat and that I would get to practice my Spanish.

Other than not being decked out in Sporting gear, she and her little clan looked like so many other people in the ground: three generations, from abuela (grandma) to nieto (grandson), gathering for the every-other-week ritual of hoping the boys on the field will do something good, maybe even inspiring, or at least win for a change. Sporting had drawn their previous game 0-0, and with a new coach this season, supporters seemed to be withholding judgment. Vamos a ver. Let’s see.

Pregame in the very red-and-white Gijón

Without knowing all of that, and before my abuela neighbor said hello, I was just enjoying watching the crowd come together, greeting each other, popping down from their seats to say hello to the friend by the aisle, commenting on this new player or that result elsewhere. Outside the stadium, the mood was relaxed. Beside the ground was a park with a bird sanctuary. Not many football grounds sit next to a wooded lake, where egrets roost in the trees postgame.

Not your typical groundhopping scenery.

It helped that it was a sunny day – not so common in this part of northern Spain, which is only four hours from Madrid but feels like Seattle to Madrid’s Dallas. Asturias has been an independent kingdom, a farming and fishing outpost, and an industrial powerhouse; for me, it’s a cool retreat from the country’s center and a stop on famous caminos, with a mile-long beach and bars and restaurants all over offering bonito, Spanish for albacore tuna.

Through all of this, one sees red and white stripes, the colors of Real Sporting Gijón. Sporting felt more present across Gijón than clubs have in most other Spanish cities I’ve visited. It’s very much a Sunderland vibe, those red and white stripes representing a collective pride, fond memories of a better past, and shared identity. Sporting once finished near the top of the league with teams built on local academy talent. They also reached consecutive Copa del Rey finals, losing to Real Madrid and Barcelona. Sporting now play in Spain’s second division, but El Molinón still looked full to me. Before the game, the announcer proudly called it Spain’s oldest football stadium still in use.

And down in the corner of this somewhat nervous scene, 20 rows off the goal line, sat me and my friendly abuela neighbor. I found out later her name was María. She and her family were en vacaciones . She enjoyed football, and we had both come a long way to spend an afternoon amid the local rituals of Sporting, cider and bonito. So let’s have fun. As the club anthem wound down and the scarves dropped, she let out a loud “Vamos, chicos!” Her grandkids chuckled at their old grandma getting into the game and chatting with her neighbor, but she whispered to me, “Son demasiados serios.” They are too serious.

¡Vamos, chicos!

The game started out even, and I told her about my team in the US, currently not great, but with a Spanish coach. She told me she always tries to get to a game when she travels – as do I. She was frustrated whenever they passed the ball al lado, or sideways, and wondered why every time the visitors’ #9 touched the ball, the stadium erupted in boos and whistles. I guessed he had played for Sporting’s rival down the road, Real Oviedo. I later learned that he had, and that he had signed for Burgos that summer despite reported interest from Sporting. He is, thus, un enemigo total. Getting the opposite treatment was another Burgos player who came up through the Sporting academy; he got a big cheer during the introductions.

(I have also seen a game in beautiful Burgos, by the way.)

Sporting started to play better, and with a confident smile, María told me “Van a ganar.” They are going to win. And one minute later, they scored! I called her una experta, and she smiled and pointed to the sky, saying she has “una conexión.” For a few minutes, the Sporting fans were up and at it, and she was clapping along, although she – and of course I – knew none of the words. The only chant I caught was “Ahora, ahora, ahora Quini ahora,” a call for Quini, Sporting’s celebrated striker of the 1970s and 80s, to bring them a goal.

Kickoff at El Molinón

As the game wore on and it stayed 1-0, tension began to mount. Few things in a sporting life are as unbearable as watching your team try to protect a one-goal lead late in the game. María showed the effects, as well; whenever Burgos came up the pitch, even when two Burgos attackers faced four defenders, she would yell “peligroso,” or dangerous! One time they got off a pretty good shot, and she took it up to “¡Peligrosísimo!” The referee made some decisions the locals didn’t like, and María joined in with waving her arms in exasperation and yelling, “¡Fuera, árbitro!” which basically means get this ref out of here.

She even taught me a new word. I try to add a new Spanish word every day, and today, thanks to María, it was guarro. I asked her what it meant, and she said “Juegan mal,” or “They are playing bad.” I looked it up later and found that guarro can mean ‘filthy’ or ‘dirty.’ María seemed to be using it for the way they played. So now I know how to say shite in Spanish, an essential skill of an international groundhopper.

A nervous corner kick late in the game.

Sporting managed to hang on and win it, hardly un clásico but tres puntos nonetheless. The reaction was more relief than joy, and María and I were both struck by how quickly the crowd emptied out of the stadium. Even the ultras, after a brief bounce-and-sing when the players came over, hustled out of there. It was 9 p.m. after all: dinner time in Spain, even on a Sunday. Bonito was in season, and the cidrerías (cider houses) were filling fast.

For me, it was another ground in La Segunda División, my fifth-straight uninspiring 1-0 result, a new corner of Spain explored, and a new entry into the top 10 stadiums I’ve been to. Mainly, though, it was learning, again, the original lesson of going to games: It’s not about the game so much as it’s about that person sitting next to you. Goals are fine, and wins for the home team are nice, but what you’ll really remember, if you’re lucky, is sharing some laughs and a bit of banter with your seat neighbor.
